title: How Much Inspection Capacity Should a City Reserve for Random Audits?
grain: One active retail-food license with a previously identified restaurant at the start of a quarter
dataset: Chicago Food Inspection Forecasting, historical permits and canvass inspections
question: How much of a city's finite inspection capacity should be reserved for random exploration?
owner: City public-health inspection and oversight team
design: Reconstruct dated permit eligibility and use only earlier restaurant records for classification, risk and geography. Compare calendar ordering, risk prioritization and stratified random exploration under one slot budget. Evaluate reordering on historically inspected premises; report worst/best bounds for missing outcomes on the full eligible roster. Supply exact inclusion probabilities for a future audit.
boundary: In the archival data only inspected restaurants reveal violations. The roster requires a known prior restaurant classification; never-classified premises are outside the target. Later inspections do not identify the causal effect of scheduling earlier.
redistribution: Deidentified derived public City of Chicago records with attribution. No names or premises addresses are published.

fields.area: Pre-specified latitude band from a prior visit
fields.days_since: Days since most recent prior observation
fields.critical_history: Earlier visits with a critical finding
fields.last_critical: Critical finding on last observed past visit
fields.outcome: Critical finding at next inspected date this quarter; empty if unlabeled
fields.inspection_day: Observed days from quarter start to first published restaurant inspection, when available

sources.license: City of Chicago open data and repository license
